title: Bollywood Bolsters Security as Shootings Revive Underworld Fears
excerpt: After gunfire at Tiger Shroff's car and a wave of extortion threats linked to the Bishnoi gang, stars are hiring bodyguards, police are telling actors to avoid crowds, and the industry is arguing over whether the 1990s are really back.
body:
• A spate of shootings and extortion threats linked by police to the Lawrence Bishnoi gang has sent Bollywood stars hiring bodyguards and cutting public appearances, AFP reports.
  • Gunfire targeted Tiger Shroff's car in Mumbai in October; police have arrested 13 people under organised crime laws and named alleged gang member Anil Pandit as wanted.
  • Mumbai Police on November 10 advised prominent actors to avoid crowded public places after investigators found the accused had scouted several stars' homes.
  • Veterans of the 1990s underworld era are split: some see a genuine revival of fear, others say copycat criminals are cashing in on the Bishnoi name.

It sounds like a Bollywood thriller, but a spate of shootings and extortion threats targeting Mumbai's stars has sent the industry scrambling for bodyguards, reviving memories of the underworld's grip on cinema in the 1990s. Police have linked the latest violence to the gang of Lawrence Bishnoi, a convicted gangster accused by US prosecutors of directing a global criminal network from behind bars, AFP reports.

Bodyguards on either side

"Stars are moving around with bodyguards on either side," actor and security agency owner Ronit Roy told AFP. "There has been a sharp increase in demand... Requests have expanded beyond just lead actors, to include family members and children." The anxiety has spilt into public view: Amitabh Bachchan recently greeted fans from behind a bulletproof enclosure outside his Mumbai home during his customary Sunday appearance, and security was beefed up around Shah Rukh Khan's home for his birthday.

The incidents behind the fear

The latest incidents include gunfire targeting actor Tiger Shroff's car in Mumbai in October and an alleged $600,000 extortion demand against actor Tusshar Kapoor, AFP reported. Police have arrested 13 people under organised crime laws in connection with the October shooting, alleging it was intended to extort money, establish gang dominance and spread fear, and have named Anil Pandit, an alleged Bishnoi gang member, as wanted. After the Shroff shooting, a social media post and audio message attributed to a Bishnoi gang associate reportedly claimed responsibility, citing the actor's closeness to Salman Khan. Bishnoi's gang has been linked to threats against Khan, reportedly over allegations that the star hunted blackbuck antelopes in 1998; Indian authorities have also accused gang members of opening fire outside Khan's Mumbai home and of involvement in the 2024 killing of politician Baba Siddique.

Police tell stars to stay out of crowds

On November 10, Mumbai Police advised prominent actors to avoid crowded public places and refrain from mingling with fans, after the investigation found the accused had conducted reconnaissance of several celebrities' homes, according to IANS. Sources in the Mumbai Crime Branch said the shooters were instructed to target celebrities whose security was relatively less stringent, and had been taken past the residences of Amitabh Bachchan, Aamir Khan, Akshay Kumar and Salman Khan. It was on October 18, IANS reported, that three motorcycle-borne men opened fire at Shroff's car in the Juhu area; the accused reportedly learned from fan reels on social media that he did not have police protection at the time.

"Some desperadoes are opening fire in the air to scare the industry and spread fear. And they have succeeded — as people have started believing that the mafia-dominated 1990s era is back."

— S. Hussain Zaidi, author and former investigative journalist, to AFP

A return of the 1990s, or copycats?

The late 1990s and early 2000s were among Bollywood's darkest periods, when syndicates led by figures such as Dawood Ibrahim used threats and violence to influence film financing, casting and distribution; the influence waned after police operations, organised-crime laws passed in 1999, and the arrival of corporate financing. Author S. Hussain Zaidi told AFP that opportunistic criminals are now exploiting established gangsters' notoriety — and noted that Bishnoi himself is in jail. Crime journalist Ahmed Ali told AFP he believed many of the calls are pranks cashing in on the situation. Producer Boney Kapoor, targeted by underworld figures in the 1990s, called the latest wave likely "short-lived" — but added: "One has to be cautious, these shootings can't be ignored."
